title: P-L-L
hook: tefillah; the verb for praying is reflexive, and many read it as judging oneself

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-U-V: teshuvah, turning and returning. Your line was turn. When the old moment came around, which way did you face? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

A woman is standing in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Her name is Hannah, and she has no children. Her lips are moving, but there's no sound. The book of Samuel says: "only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard." The priest Eli watches her, decides she's drunk, and tells her to put away her wine. She isn't drunk. She's pouring out her heart. The text says she "prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." Silent, inward, completely honest. What she was doing has a Hebrew word, and its three letters are today's root.
screen: `HANNAH AT SHILOH.` → `LIPS MOVING, NO VOICE.` → `ELI THINKS SHE'S DRUNK.`

segments.voice: P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed. From it comes tefillah, prayer. Turn it four ways. First, the courtroom. In Exodus, a fine is set, and a man "shall pay as the judges determine." The Hebrew behind judges there is from this root. The letters have to do with judging, weighing, deciding. Second, one verse that holds both. In the book of Samuel, Eli warns his sons: "If one man sin against another, the judge shall judge him: but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him?" Judge, and intreat, which means plead or pray. The same letters, a few words apart. Third, the form of the verb. To pray, in Hebrew, is l'hitpallel, built in a form Hebrew often uses for actions turned back on oneself, like getting dressed or washing up. Some teachers read it this way: to pray is to judge yourself, to stand in front of the truth about your own life. Others hear it as standing before the Judge, or as pleading. These readings sit side by side, and they don't cancel each other out. Fourth, Hannah. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, draws lessons about prayer from her: say the words in the heart, let the lips move, keep the voice low. Her prayer wasn't a performance for Eli or anyone. It was a long, honest look inward, said to God. So the root gives prayer a mirror as well as a window.
screen: `AS THE JUDGES DETERMINE.` · `JUDGE AND INTREAT, ONE VERSE.` · `A VERB TURNED BACK ON ONESELF.` · `HANNAH'S SILENT PRAYER.` · then, large: `PRAYER LOOKS INWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: an honest look, the way Hannah prayed. Settle, and breathe. Let your face go still. Ask yourself one plain question about the last day: where was I at my best, and where did I fall short? Don't argue with the answer or dress it up. Just look, the way a fair judge looks: clearly, without cruelty. Then let it rest. If you pray, you can bring what you saw into your prayer, with your lips moving and your voice low, the way Hannah did. If you don't, simply stay with what's true for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
P-L-L. Pe, lamed, lamed: to judge, to plead, and in its turned-back form, to pray. The root of tefillah. Today's word.
Your line: prayer looks inward. Today, before you ask for anything, from God or anyone, take one honest look at your own part first. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah, the standing prayer of the daily services, quietly, with the lips moving and the voice low, a practice the Talmud draws from Hannah's prayer.

what a scholar hears: 1 Samuel 2:25 uses the root for 'judge' and 'intreat' in one verse; Berakhot learns how to pray from Hannah's silent lips.
